fatal_errors: The proposed entropy-stabilized sluggish-diffusion mechanism is the opposite of the observed non-sluggish diffusion and kinetically controlled surface segregation.
The prediction of preserved composition and morphology contradicts the observed Au/Cu surface segregation, melting or evaporation, particle loss, reshaping, and approximately 22% size reduction.
The intervention does not reconstruct the controlled in situ vacuum-heating experiment on sub-10 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.

Changing mixing, cooling, or pre-segregation simultaneously changes initial composition profiles, defects, phases, and morphology, so it does not isolate configurational entropy as the causal variable.
No cited evidence supports the claim that configurational entropy directly raises atomic diffusion barriers.
explanation: The response addresses thermal stability of near-equiatomic multielement nanoparticles and proposes a falsifiable comparison, but it misses the specific AuCoCuNiPt system, FCC multi-twinned or icosahedral initial structure, PLD preparation, vacuum ramp to 973 K, stepped in situ STEM-EDS analysis, and molecular-dynamics component. More importantly, it elevates the conventional high-entropy/sluggish-diffusion expectation into the hypothesis, whereas the target evidence rejects that expectation: diffusion becomes active above roughly 673 K, surface-energy differences drive Au and Cu outward, and shape evolution enhances local transport before melting and evaporation. Its broad service-temperature range and exclusion of reactive atmospheres provide only weak condition and boundary agreement. The proposed high-mixing versus intentionally inhomogeneous comparison is also substantially confounded and lacks direct measurements of species-resolved self-diffusivity and its correlation with shape and surface composition. Thus it is testable in a generic sense but neither an accurate reconstruction nor an evidence-supported alternative.
